stem: A client with chemotherapy-induced oral mucositis has painful oral ulcers but can still tolerate gentle toothbrushing. Which oral-care plan is most appropriate?

options.A: Use a soft-bristle toothbrush for gentle tooth cleaning, rinse frequently with a bland solution or plain water, keep the oral tissues moist, and use prescribed pain relief as needed.
options.B: Use foam swabs instead of a toothbrush for routine tooth cleaning, rinse with a bland solution, and continue this approach until the oral ulcers have healed.
options.C: Use a soft-bristle toothbrush for the teeth, then rinse several times each day with an alcohol-containing mouthwash to reduce bacteria around the ulcers.
options.D: Pause toothbrushing while the ulcers remain painful, use bland rinses for comfort, and restart mechanical tooth cleaning after the oral mucosa begins to heal.

rationale: Current National Cancer Institute guidance for oral mucositis supports continued gentle oral hygiene with a soft-bristle toothbrush, frequent mild or bland rinses, moisture maintenance, and pain-relief measures. The NCI health-professional PDQ states that foam-swab brushes do not effectively clean teeth and should not routinely replace a soft nylon-bristled toothbrush. NCI also advises avoiding alcohol-containing mouthwashes in clients with oral complications. Therefore A is correct. B substitutes an ineffective routine method for tooth cleaning, C adds an irritating alcohol-containing rinse, and D unnecessarily stops tolerated mechanical cleaning.
educational_objective: For chemotherapy-induced oral mucositis, continue gentle mechanical tooth cleaning with a soft toothbrush when tolerated, use frequent bland rinses and moisture/pain measures, and avoid routine foam-swab substitution or alcohol-containing mouthwash.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Oral Complications of Cancer Therapies (PDQ®) — Health Professional Version; Oral Complications of Cancer Therapies (PDQ®) — Patient Version
source_locator: Health Professional PDQ > Oral hygiene/basic oral care and oral mucositis: use a soft toothbrush to maintain oral hygiene; foam-swab brushes do not effectively clean teeth and should not be a routine substitute for a soft nylon-bristled toothbrush; frequent bland saline and/or sodium-bicarbonate rinses clean and lubricate tissues; commercial mouthwashes with an alcohol base or astringent properties are not recommended for patients with oral complications; analgesic therapy is used as needed. Patient PDQ > Care of mucositis during chemotherapy and radiation therapy > Cleaning the mouth: use a soft-bristle toothbrush, mild rinses or plain water, keep the mouth moist, avoid alcohol-containing rinses, and clean the mouth regularly.
source_claim_supported: Oral mucositis care includes gentle soft-bristle tooth cleaning when tolerated, frequent bland rinses and moisture/pain measures; foam swabs should not routinely replace effective tooth brushing, and alcohol-containing mouthwashes should be avoided.

supporting_sources.organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
supporting_sources.document_title: Oral Complications of Cancer Therapies (PDQ®) — Patient Version
supporting_sources.locator: Care of mucositis during chemotherapy and radiation therapy > Cleaning the mouth: clean teeth and mouth regularly; use a soft-bristle toothbrush; use mild rinses or plain water; keep the mouth moist; avoid rinses containing alcohol.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Gentle brushing, mild rinses, moisture maintenance, and avoidance of alcohol-containing rinses are appropriate during mucositis.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort, printed p. 35: provide comfort and assistance in activities of daily living; perform skin/tissue assessment and implement measures to maintain tissue integrity; provide nonpharmacological comfort measures; assess client for pain and intervene as appropriate.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — oral hygiene and comfort measures for chemotherapy-induced mucositis
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four oral-care plans to remove the absolute-word cue and make the distractors clinically plausible. The revised item preserves gentle brushing, bland rinsing, moisture maintenance, and pain-control concepts while testing realistic errors involving foam-swab substitution, alcohol-containing mouthwash, and unnecessary suspension of tolerated mechanical cleaning.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Cancer therapy adverse effects — oral mucositis hygiene and comfort
audit_findings.stem: PASS — chemotherapy-induced mucositis is explicit, and tolerance of gentle toothbrushing removes ambiguity about whether brushing must be withheld.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects NCI-supported gentle brushing, bland rinsing, moisture maintenance, and pain management; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — bland rinsing is appropriate, but routine foam-swab substitution does not effectively clean teeth and is not recommended in place of a soft toothbrush.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — soft brushing is appropriate, but an alcohol-containing mouthwash is specifically discouraged for oral complications.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — bland rinses are appropriate, but stopping mechanical tooth cleaning is unnecessary when the client can tolerate gentle brushing.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option containing the supported oral-care measures without adding a contradictory practice.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B substitutes ineffective tooth cleaning, C adds an irritating alcohol rinse, and D stops tolerated mechanical cleaning.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all options are similar in length and clinical detail and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort directly includes ADL assistance, comfort measures, tissue-integrity measures, and pain intervention.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether foam swabs or temporary cessation of brushing could be justified because of painful ulcers; the stem explicitly states brushing is tolerated and NCI states foam swabs do not effectively clean teeth, leaving A uniquely best.
